headline: Matthew Cobb On Genetics' Moral Reckonings
tldr: Zoologist Matthew Cobb explains why gene editing keeps forcing scientists into self-imposed pauses -- and why the public still isn't in the room when it matters.
summary: Kiki interviews British zoologist Matthew Cobb, professor of zoology at the University of Manchester, about his new book 'As Gods: A Moral History of the Genetic Age,' which traces the ethical reckonings of genetic science from the 1970s to today.

Cobb describes blending science and humanities since school and spending 45 years studying drosophila. His interest in science history was sparked when research on 'the maggot's nose' led him into a 17th-century archive at London's Natural History Museum.

The book's core theme is that scientists have paused their own genetics research four separate times out of fear -- unique among all fields, even the Manhattan Project. The 1975 Asilomar meeting focused entirely on lab safety, not whether the research should happen at all, and excluded the public. The resulting controversy faded by 1980, just as Genentech and Apple went public the same week and Reagan-era deregulation began.

Cobb details the 2018 He Jiankui scandal, in which a Chinese scientist edited the genes of embryos that became three girls with unpredictable, heritable mutations. Unlike earlier eras, no moratorium followed -- CRISPR co-inventors Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier disagreed over whether to call for one, and Cobb argues embryo editing mostly serves a tiny number of wealthy Western couples.

The conversation closes on gene drives, weighed against roughly 600,000 malaria deaths a year against unknown ecological risks and possibly simpler fixes like a new WHO-approved vaccine. Cobb argues genuine local consent is nearly impossible and calls for an international regulatory body similar to civil aviation or atomic energy oversight.
mindmap:
# As Gods: The Moral History of Genetics

## Matthew Cobb's Path to Science History
- Mixed science and humanities in UK schooling
- Studying drosophila fruit flies for 45 years
- Maggot's nose research led to 17th century archives
- Found astonishing texts at Natural History Museum library

## Genetics' Self-Imposed Moratoriums
- Four times scientists paused their own research
- Unique among sciences, not even the Manhattan Project
- Asilomar meetings in 1972 and 1975
  - About 200 scientists at a California cinema
  - Discussion focused on safety, not on rightness
  - Public and journalists largely absent
- Public backlash followed
  - Cambridge Massachusetts town halls over Harvard lab
  - Protests faded by 1980 as fears eased
- 1980: Genentech and Apple go public same week
  - Reagan-era deregulation begins
  - Human gene in bacteria proved harmless

## The He Jiankui CRISPR Scandal
- 2018 Chinese scientist edited embryo genes
- Three girls born with novel, patchy mutations
- Mutations now heritable, could spread through generations
- No moratorium resulted, unlike earlier eras
- Doudna and Charpentier split on calling for pause
- Called "an answer in search of a question"

## Gene Drives and Global Risk
- 600,000 people, mostly children, die of malaria yearly
- Gene drives could eliminate mosquitoes, risk unknown ecology
- New WHO malaria vaccine may be simpler fix
- Kevin Esvelt grew frightened of his own work
- t-CRISPR now targets invasive house mice in Australia/NZ

## Longtermism and Future Humanity
- Effective altruists prioritize far future over present people
- Cobb argues climate action matters more than gene tinkering

## The Missing Public Voice
- No case of public truly co-deciding gene tech
- Gene drive trials need consent from illiterate villages
- Proposal: body like civil aviation or atomic energy authority

stickies.text: This book, the subtitle really should be a critical history, but you couldn't call it that in a popular trade book.
Four times scientists have called a research moratorium out of fear -- no other field has ever done that.
600,000 people a year die of malaria, the vast majority children under five.
Human embryo editing is a solution in search of an answer -- sorry, an answer in search of a question.
The bacterium wouldn't know what to do with a human gene, so the feared experiment turned out harmless.
Those girls didn't ask to have their genes changed -- somebody did it to them.
I want people to know what is being discussed, and to think about what the alternatives might be.

receipts.title: Self-regulation left the public out
receipts.detail: Cobb argues the 1975 Asilomar meeting focused only on safety and never asked whether the research should happen, while public voices were absent entirely.

receipts.title: This is too important for scientists alone
receipts.detail: Pushing back on reviews calling his book negative, Cobb says his real point is that genetics decisions shouldn't be left solely to scientists.

receipts.title: The He Jiankui case stank from the start
receipts.detail: Cobb says there was no medical need for the experiment, and the scientific community was complicit by embracing a vague 'prudent path' toward embryo editing beforehand.

receipts.title: Doudna is wrong to call it too late
receipts.detail: Cobb disagrees with Jennifer Doudna's view that a moratorium is now pointless, noting Emmanuelle Charpentier did sign the call for a pause.

receipts.title: Longtermists misdirect their brilliance
receipts.detail: Cobb admires effective altruists' concern for humanity's future but argues their money and vision should target climate and carbon economies, not gene tinkering.

receipts.title: Gene drive scientists aren't reckless
receipts.detail: Cobb defends gene-drive researchers as deeply concerned rather than cavalier, citing Kevin Esvelt's fear after grasping the technology's implications.

receipts.title: Sexy tech fixes can eclipse simpler answers
receipts.detail: Cobb argues the appeal of elegant solutions like gene drives or mRNA vaccines can distract from more mundane but effective options, such as a new malaria vaccine.

receipts.title: No one has really let the public decide
receipts.detail: Cobb says he can't name a case where the public and scientists genuinely co-decided a genetic technology's future, despite past debates like Cambridge's.

receipts.title: Local consent for gene drives is nearly impossible
receipts.detail: Cobb notes villages targeted for malaria gene drives may lack a word for 'gene,' and mosquitoes cross borders anyway, so no single community can consent for a global release.

receipts.title: Genetics needs its own aviation authority
receipts.detail: Cobb proposes an international regulatory body modeled on civil aviation or atomic energy oversight, though he doubts governments currently want that.
